touches.text: A machine the device owns that has settings is reached through its device, with the same help/list/show/get/set: cairn <device> <machine> <command> (eg cairn cairn scheduler list). The bus only ever sees the device, which passes the rest down.
Every verb anywhere is reached from the cairn command, as a path: cairn <device> [<machine> ...] <verb>. There is no central list.

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.

INTENTION: "HARBOR MASTER IS A REPORTING SYSTEM AND NOTHING MORE. IT REPORTS WHERE EVERYTHING IS AND NOTHING ELSE PERIOD." It owns no gates and controls nothing. It keeps the register of every ticket: open, at sea, in port. Task, trouble and fixit tickets show there too; inference tickets do not.
TOOLS: base, artifact, charter, operator_inbox, proof_coverage, question, system_word; machine learning_block.

VERBS: status queries only (show, get), and crossing, the notice a ticket sends as it moves, which keeps the register. It answers no gate and moves no ticket. A ticket that would cross a gate asks that gate itself for an inspection, and either receives a pass or sends itself back to design (3.3.4). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "why would the harbor master's bus face answer anything other than a status query. if anything (ticket) is going to try and cross a gate it's the ticket that asks that gate for an inspection. and the ticket either recieves a pass or it sends itself back to design." Measured the same day: the bus face also answers `clear` (fires clearance.py and moves a boat) and `watch` (sends a ticket to FIXME), and both leave. COMMANDS: cairn codemother harbor_master -> "652 boats (570 open, 82 in port)".
bus_client: gets a process onto the bus (reach a device, or connect). Its connect is a wake attempt (5.3.5.1). USERS: every process that speaks.

conflicts.ticket_says: any other verb exits 2 naming 9.4.1.5 — non-status verbs like clear and watch will be rejected with exit code 2
conflicts.why: The outline's Measured section at 9.4.1.5 documents that 'the bus face also answers `clear` (fires clearance.py and moves a boat) and `watch` (sends a ticket to FIXME)', but the ticket's implementation exits with error 2 for any non-status verb. This prevents clear and watch from being routed to harbor_master, contradicting the outline's documented behavior.
